newsitem.title: FRANCE: Some French ministers favour a weak euro--Le Monde.
newsitem.headline: Some French ministers favour a weak euro--Le Monde.

text.p: Some ministers in France's conservative government believe the future European single currency should be depreciated against the dollar, afternoon daily Le Monde said on Monday.
The opposition Socialist party has already suggested that the new euro should be at parity with the dollar -- implying a fairly significant devaluation against the U.S. currency.
The European currency unit, against which the euro is will be exchanged on a one-for-one basis, is currently worth $1.27.

"In private, some ministers in (Prime Minister) Alain Juppe's government express the same wish -- the euro, from January 1, 1999, must be pushed lower so that it can be used as a trade tool," Le Monde said.

The newspaper noted that the future European Central Bank, which will be modelled on the German Bundesbank and likewise based in Frankfurt, could fight any devaluation in the euro on the grounds that this could fuel inflation.
The central bank will be required by law to maintain price stability.
However, Le Monde argued, the launch of the euro would create a giant European market which, like the huge U.S. market, would be relatively immune to outside influences.
"The risk of imported inflation in the case of a competitive devaluation in the euro would in this way, be sharply reduced," it said.

French ministers have said repeatedly that they believe the dollar is undervalued against European currencies. Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said last week, however, that it was up to financial markets to fix the dollar-euro exchange rate.
